text:
Sir, I’m genuinely disappointed this time. The film is just average — it depends entirely on marketing magic rather than offering a real cinematic experience. Honestly, Thamma was far better than this mindless and pointless film.

Yash sir is undoubtedly a talented actor, but if he truly wants to grow into a great artist, he should consider distancing himself from these producers who are simply cashing in on his name. In this movie, his dialogues sounded exaggerated and overconfident, which made the character feel unnatural and forced.

The storyline lacked any solid foundation or logic. Why is a teacher suddenly taking such actions in a random village, and why do the villagers agree so easily? The mall scene — where Yash’s character takes someone’s baby without reason — was completely absurd. The dialogues were illogical, and none of the female characters stood out; perhaps they were overshadowed by Yash’s over-the-top portrayal.

Overall, this film is built on pointless writing and direction with zero logic or emotional depth. It’s hard to believe it was made by Jay Bodas, the same filmmaker who gave us Fakt Mahilao Maate, a genuinely good film. Sadly, it feels like many are now prioritizing money over meaningful storytelling.

Producers like Vaishal Shah are, in fact, more harmful to the Gujarati film industry than others — because he has the power and resources to create truly great cinema, yet he chooses to settle for making mediocre, mindless films that survive purely on marketing gimmicks. It’s disappointing to see such potential wasted.

I now have even greater respect for filmmakers like KD, Abhishek Shah, and Manish Saini — they stay true to their craft and consistently bring something fresh and thoughtful to the audience.

As for Vaishal Shah’s claim of making a ₹100 crore Gujarati film — with this kind of substandard work, that seems impossible. And I must say, I’m also disappointed with the reviewers; this film is, at best, moderately entertaining and deserves no more than 2 to 2.5 stars.

Every frame reflects faith in the story being told, and a quiet courage to say something meaningful in a time dominated by surface-level cinema.
